feed.title: PatchLabs changelog
feed.subtitle: What PatchLabs shipped, and when. Real entries only.

entry.title: Our sign-in form can no longer be used to email strangers
entry.summary: Our own logs showed a bot typing other people's addresses into the sign-in form since 10 Nov (about 45 unwanted sign-in emails; three opened by mail scanners, creating empty accounts). The form now needs a signed one-time challenge with a small proof of work and a short wait, catches form-filling bots with a hidden field, caps links to new addresses per hour, and a link signs in only when a person clicks Continue.

entry.title: The revert test, 36 hours on: still readable, and the Activity page lists the id
entry.summary: 36 hours after a force-push removed it, the demo token in our public test repo was still readable without login from the commit page (full, 7- and 4-character id), the raw file and the REST API. The repo's public Activity page and /activity API list the force-push with the full id of the removed commit. Revoke first.

entry.title: A revert is not a rotation: the Together AI case, tested on GitHub
entry.summary: Together AI disclosed on 21 Nov that an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public repo; the commit was reverted and prompt samples were still downloaded. In a public test repo, a commit removed by force-push stayed readable without a login from four characters of its id. Revoke first, then clean up.

entry.title: PL-040: hijacked third-party scripts, and a guide to the Optimizely compromise
entry.summary: The free headers check now flags pages that load scripts from other sites with no Content-Security-Policy limit on where they can send data (PL-040). The guide covers the 16 Nov Optimizely compromise (178+ organisations) and a Chrome test: a script-src allow-list alone let a script send data out four ways; default-src 'self' stopped all four.

entry.title: The two-account test, at the scale of a real breach: the credit union case
entry.summary: Payee records from about 40 Irish credit unions were exposed by a signed-in attacker whose script made five million requests against an authorization flaw (BleepingComputer, 18 Nov). What it means for AI-built apps: signed in proves nothing, one leaking request means every row, and logs decide whether you can tell people what was taken.

entry.title: Guide: why can my users see each other's data? The two-account test
entry.summary: A ten-minute test with two accounts, a SQL query that lists read policies which never check the user, the fix, the secret-key server-route trap, and a test that keeps it fixed. Run on Postgres 17 and 18.

entry.title: Check a whole list of sites at once, on Apify
entry.summary: The PatchLabs Actor on Apify grades a list of sites for HTTPS, certificate, security headers and cookies, and scans each page's scripts for leaked secret keys, shown masked. https://apify.com/patchlabs/ai-app-security-check

entry.title: Code checks catch logins that store passwords in plain text
entry.summary: New check PL-039 in patchlabs-cli v0.6.0 and the hosted Code check: a login query that matches on the password, an unhashed password insert, or a plain password column. Clean on ten real projects (cal.com, Payload, Directus and others); flagged all six sampled public repos with the pattern. Guide: how to check and move to Supabase Auth.

entry.title: Code checks catch personal data sent to AI models; a leak must be shown before we call it one
entry.summary: Hosted checks now flag personal data in request headers or AI prompts (PL-037) and keys in Claude Code settings files (PL-009). Proven findings now require the lab to reproduce the leak first; tables that only look open are reported as unproven. The hosted Code check is now copied from the open-source patchlabs-cli at a pinned release and compared with the latest CLI every six hours, so free and paid checks find the same things. Teams: the free RLS check and patchlabs-cli flag members tables any signed-in user can write to, letting them join any team (PL-038).

entry.title: PatchLabs v3: four product lines, and checks that read your code
entry.summary: Four product lines (Lab, Code, Fix, Watch). PatchLabs Code reads the repo on every check: secret keys in code (PL-009), open Edge Functions using the service key (PL-017), sign-ups without email confirmation (PL-018), roles in user_metadata (PL-019), browser-only admin checks (PL-020), unverified payment webhooks (PL-021), trusted user ids (PL-022), vulnerable dependencies via OSV (PL-023), raw HTML (PL-024), open Firebase rules (PL-025), risky CORS (PL-026). One finding format across report and API. Findings library PL-001 to PL-026 and Learn guides. Demo, integrations and solutions pages. Coming, not shipped: Lab checks PL-012 to PL-016; automatic pull requests with the GitHub App.

entry.title: PatchLabs v2: accounts, monitoring and proof anyone can verify
entry.summary: New website; email-link accounts and workspaces; monitoring with weekly or monthly re-checks, diffs, email alerts and Slack-compatible webhooks; badges and public status; Ed25519-signed receipts; owner decisions and answers; REST API and API keys; remote MCP server; free RLS check with no sign-up; one-click commit of the fix on GitHub; plans.

entry.title: First public leak checks
entry.summary: Public leak checks from a GitHub repo with ownership proof, reports by email and a spend cap per check. Autonomous run on 20 new apps: 18 of 20 fixes passed the strict lab proof with no human (n=20); 15 needed only the smallest model; median 3.5 minutes per app.

entry.title: Fix agents re-verified: 19 of 20 worked first time
entry.summary: We re-verified 20 real fixes written by our agents: 19 of 20 worked first time and applied cleanly (n=20, 5 Nov 2026).
